When you use the copy mechanism, you can set the scaling parameter as fixed or let it vary.

Old style:
f(...,copy=..., fixed=FALSE)

New style:
f(...,copy=..., hyper=list(beta=list(fixed=FALSE)))

New style lets you specify the distribution and various other things.

There's no mechanism to multiply more complicated random effects, so I don't think it's possible to have covariates.

Thanks! And one can simply add more terms, so the code below works.

Alas this is a side project, so I might not get back to it for a couple of weeks. The slides look useful: I also saw mention of marked point processes, which is something else I'll want for another project. I'll have to download them & read through them on my next trip to London.

set.seed(6996)
NYear1=2000; K1=100; alpha1=0.5; beta1=0.1; sigma1=0.2

x1=numeric(NYear1)
T1=rnorm(NYear1)
x1[1] <- rnorm(1, log(K1), 1)
for(t in 2:NYear1) {
  x1[t] <- log(K1) + (alpha1+beta1*T1[t])*(x1[t-1]-log(K1)) + rnorm(1,0,sigma1)
}
N1 <- rpois(NYear1, exp(x1))

Y1=cbind(c(N1, rep(NA, length(N1)-1)), # data
        rep(c(NA,0), times=c(length(N1), length(N1)-1))) # zeroes for state
Data1=data.frame(Y=Y1,
                t=c(1:length(N1), 2:length(N1)),
                lag1=c(rep(NA,length(N1)), 2:length(N1)-1),
                lag1a=c(rep(NA,length(N1)), 2:length(N1)-1),
                Temp=c(rep(NA,length(N1)), 10*T1[-1]),
                shock=c(rep(NA,length(N1)), 1:(length(N1)-1))
)

# Fit latent model
formula1 = Y ~ f(t, model="iid", fixed=TRUE) + f(lag1, copy="t", hyper=list(beta=list(fixed=FALSE))) +
                        f(lag1a, Temp, copy="t", hyper=list(beta=list(fixed=FALSE))) +  f(shock, model ="iid")
Gomp1 = inla(formula1, data = Data1,family = c("poisson", "gaussian"),
            control.family = list(list(), list(initial=10, fixed=T)))
summary(Gomp1)$hyperpar

If you compare models with

y ~ f(, model="rw2")

against

y ~ f(, model="rw2") + f(, model="rw2")

using mlik, you'll need to include the term 0.5*log(|R|). yes

if the rw2 is defined on integers, then

INLA:::inla.rw <http://inla.rw>(n, order = 1L, sparse = TRUE, scale.model = FALSE)

will compute the R, and scaled if scale.model=TRUE, and you can then
compute the missing term using

my.determinant = function(
        A,
        tol = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps),
        log=FALSE,
        rankdef)
{
    X = svd(A)
    d = X$d
    if (!missing(rankdef)) {
        d = sort(X$d)[-(1:rankdef)]
    } else {
        d = X$d[X$d > max(tol * X$d[1L], 0.0)]
    }
    if (log) {
        return (sum(log(d)))
    } else {
        return (prod(d))
    }
}

The missing term is part of the normalizing constant for the RW2 term.

beta0<- 0.01

b0<- 0.3950659

# Initial values from fitdistr

a0<- 3.2395390
b0<- 0.3950659

beta<-numeric(iter) # iter= Number of iteration
beta<-c()
beta[1]<-b0
alpha<-numeric(iter)
alpha<-c()
alpha[1]<-a0

# Matrix that will contain recorded draws:

alpha[i]
else
alpha[i-1]
accept<-accept+1

draws[i,1]<-beta[i]
draws[i,2]<-alpha[i]
}
# End MCMC Loop
}

This is possible, due to how the numerics is implemented internally.
Usually, the difference is within numerical tolerance, but for large
models with hard to identify parameters, the optimisation may terminate
at a different place when the prediction part is included.
Which category your model falls into depends on how much and in what way
your results differ.

A more stable, and generally faster, approach is to make two inla()
calls, where only the second includes the prediction, is started at the
precious parameter estimate (and restart=FALSE to prevent further
optimsation).  I believe there is a FAQ entry on this.

Finn

Since the two calls don't have the same model size you need to
specifically extract the estimated theta-vector instead of using the
whole "res5" structure.  The documentation has this:

which method is actually correct in the current package version.)

> On Sun, 2012-04-01 at 00:46 -0700, Chris wrote:
> > Hi all,
> > I've been trying for a week to work around this error.
> >
> >
> > #####
> > file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: 64e669042e54  date: Fri Mar 16 12:57:24 2012
> > +0100
> > Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 780, Thread:
> > 0
> > Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...
>
>
> When we get 'Fail to factorize Q' it means that the precision matrix is
> numerically singular. In most cases it is not, but it can still be so
> numerically for some ''almost ill-defined models''.
>
> When the precision matrix *is* singular, this is usually due to the
> improper default prior for the intercept, so setting
> control.fixed=list(prec.intecept=0.001), or similar, will solve the
> issue.
>
> the intrinsic models, are almost singular, as they have a constr=TRUE
> default, which ensure they are not. However, numerically, they are
> computed without the constraint and then we correct for the constraint.
> this means there are some small epsilons around to make non-sinuglar.
> This the argument 'diagonal=' in the 'f()', which is default 1e-6 for
> intrinsic models. This constant can be to small in some cases.
>
>
> so, increasing the diagonal argument and setting a proper prior for the
> intercept, solves the issue.
>
> set.seed (1)
> n <- 500
> t <- 25 ## n observations per loc
> y <- rnorm(n*t)
> x <- y+rnorm(n*t)
> t2 <- rep(1:t,each=n)
> id <- rep(1:n,each=t)
>
> data <- data.frame("y"=y, "x"=x, "t2"=t2, "id"=id)
> A = matrix(runif(n^2), n, n)
> B <-inla.matrix2graph(A) # tried as a grap
>
> diag.eps = 1e-4
> test <- inla(y~x+f(id, model="besag", graph=B, diagonal=diag.eps)+
>              f(t2, model="rw2", diagonal = diag.eps),
>              data=data, family="gaussian",
>              verbose=T,
>              control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.01))
>
>
> rho = 0.9 ## sparse matrix example
> Q = toeplitz(c(1+rho^2, -rho,  rep(0, n-3), -rho)) / (1-rho^2)
> Q = inla.as.dgTMatrix(Q)
>
> diag.eps = 1e-3
> test2 <- inla(y~x+f(id, model="besag", graph=Q,  diagonal=diag.eps) +
>               f(t2, model="rw2", diagonal=diag.eps),
>               data=data, family="gaussian",
>               verbose=TRUE,
>               keep=TRUE,
>               control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.01))

form=value~ -1 +

      f(GISID, model="iid", hyper = list(prec = list( initial = log(0.000001), fixed = TRUE))) +

out=inla(form=form, family = "poisson", E=TOT_POP, data = prddat,

          control.inla = list( strategy = "laplace", int.strategy = "eb"),

          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),

          control.compute=list(dic=FALSE, config=TRUE), verbose=FALSE)

   xx=inla.posterior.sample(nsample, out)

The funny thing is that it will run for 3-4 iterations,  then crash with the above message.

I have also tried with a number of 'default' settings in control.inla and control.compute.

Any suggestions would be vary helpful

messages.body_plain:
Dear R-INLA Group,
Please, I wish to analyse a spatial data using R-INLA  through multilevel approach with my main primary objective been to interpolate for observed/unobserved locations in my study region (using joint Gaussian distribution) and plotting the predicted values with their prediction variances/standard errors on a grid.
Children in my data set are nested within households in the study locations and my multilevel model (without spatial) showed significant household random effects hence my choice to employ spatial analysis with multilevel approach.
The need to include household random effects in my spatial model makes it a bit difficult for me to implement in R unlike the standard geostatistical analysis.
I have a data frame containing my geographical coordinates (x=longitude and y=latitude) as well as my response and covariates.
The spatial mixed effects model I wish to fit and interpolate is: Yij(t) = Xij(t)β +hj+S(t)+Ɛij           (1)
where i=individual child, j=household, X(t)= spatial referenced non-random covariates, S(t)= spatially correlated stationary Gaussian process.
Ɛij =nugget effect/measurement error, Yij(t) = response of child i in household j at location t and my response is a continuous variable, hj =household level random effects and β=regression coefficients (spatial trend parameter).
Specifically, S(t)~N(0,σ2H11(ɸ) ), where σ2  is the variance (partial sill),  H11(ɸ) is the correlation matrix based on valid correlation function h(u; ɸ), where u is the distance between locations and ɸ is the correlation parameter (range).
hj~N(0, σ2h), where σ2h is the household level variance (ie, hj is normally distributed with zero mean and variance σ2h).
Ɛij~N(0,τ2), where τ2 is the nugget effect/measurement error (ie, Ɛij is normally distributed with zero mean and variance τ2).

I am trying to achieve the above task through geostatistical analysis but other methods which can be implemented in R are also welcomed.

Please, could somebody help me with some papers in the literature, existing R code in R-INLA which are related to my problem as well as providing me with R codes to implement this assuming someone has already done this kind of multilevel spatial regression and interpolation in R.
For the purpose of reproducibility, I have attached my data frame (d1.RData) as described above for any help. My outcome variable in the dataset is haz2 and is continuous, my covariates of interest are m5newf, v445new, hw1new, v012, v190newf, b0new, v481new and m18new. The household identifier is hhid and my spatial coordinates are x and y for longitude and latitude respectively.

Many thanks for your help in advance.

Justice
